newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada to pursue forestry standards at G7.
newsitem.headline: Canada to pursue forestry standards at G7.

text.p: Canada expects to butt heads with the United States at the Denver G7 summit this week over Canada's plan to pursue a global forestry convention, Canadian officials said this week.
"Just so that there's no illusion here, the forestry convention is running into very heavy weather with the Americans," said one senior official, who asked not to be identified.

Among Canada's top priorities at the Group of Seven summit will be rallying support for a legally binding global forestry convention to set internationally accepted standards to ensure the industry is environmentally sustainable.
Canadian officials and analysts said the convention would benefit Canada, one of the world's biggest exporters of forestry products.

John Kirton, director of the G7 research group at the University of Toronto, said Canadian companies must cope with strict and often expensive regulations not faced by competitors in other countries. Legally binding international standards would force foreign competitors to come into line with Canada, he said.
Canada has won the backing of all other G7 members for its global forestry initiative, except the United States.
"The Americans have a belief that the forestry convention would not serve the purposes that we believe it would serve," said another Canadian official.
While the United States has said it wanted to pursue sustainable forest management, it was not convinced a global forestry convention would achieve that.

"Rather than dissipate energy on a forest convention -- which would undoubtedly be costly and time-consuming -- it would be far more useful to build on the momentum already achieved" in existing treaties and talks, U.S. Undersecretary of State for Global Affairs Tim Wirth said in a speech in in April.
The Canadian officials acknowledged that without U.S. support, progress on a forestry accord at the G7 summit would be difficult.
"I would not want you to think that there's any guarantee that this is an achievable one," said the official. "We're going to work hard on it."
